title: Chocolate Bread Pudding
status: Complete editorial review; accepted locally; publication pending
scope: Resolution of an individually held recipe following direct user decisions; no kitchen test

exactBefore.body:
## Chef's Note

Bread pudding is a way to honor stale bread - brioche is rich and tender, so it soaks up custard without becoming mushy. The double chocolate (bittersweet and white) creates complexity: dark chocolate for depth, white chocolate for sweetness. The 15-minute soak before baking is mandatory - it lets the bread fully hydrate so the custard distributes evenly and the whole thing sets together.

## Directions

1.  **Prep:** Preheat oven to 350°F. Spray eight 6-oz ramekins (or a 9x13 baking dish) with non-stick spray.
2.  **The Mix:** In a large bowl, toss the brioche cubes with the chopped bittersweet chocolate and white chocolate chips.
3.  **The Custard:** In a mixer, beat eggs, 1/2 cup sugar, and vanilla until pale. Gradually whisk in the heavy cream and milk until smooth.
4.  **The Soak:** Pour the custard over the bread mixture. Toss gently to coat. **Let stand for 15 minutes** to allow the brioche to hydrate.
5.  **Assemble:** Transfer the mixture to the prepared ramekins, spreading evenly. Drizzle the remaining 4 tbsp of sugar over the tops.
6.  **Bake:** Bake for 15-20 minutes until the edges are golden and the custard is set in the center but still has a slight wobble.
7.  **Serve:** Serve warm with a generous scoop of vanilla bean ice cream.

frontmatter.title: Chocolate Bread Pudding
frontmatter.cookTime: About 35–60 min for cups or 45–60 min for a larger dish
frontmatter.totalTime: About 1¾–2¼ hr, including soaking and a 10-minute rest
ingredients: nonstick cooking spray, enough to coat all baking dishes
453 g (1 lb) brioche, cut into ½-inch cubes; measure the bread by weight
1/2 cup unsweetened cocoa powder, Dutch-process or natural
frontmatter.source: Mise double-chocolate adaptation of King Arthur Test Kitchen’s bread pudding

ingredients.name: nonstick cooking spray
ingredients.allowance: enough to coat all baking dishes

ingredients.name: brioche
ingredients.preparation: cut into ½-inch cubes; measure the bread by weight

steps.title: Choose dishes with room for the full batch
steps.text: Use oven-safe individual soufflé cups with at least 12 fluid ounces (1½ cups) capacity each. Coat them with {{ingredients}} and set them on a rimmed baking sheet. Use enough cups for the whole batch. Fill no cup above three-quarters of its capacity after soaking, and have an extra cup or small dish ready if needed. For a larger pudding, use a coated 2-quart baking dish only if the complete soaked mixture fits with space below its rim; use an extra dish for any excess.

steps.title: Combine the bread and chocolate pieces
steps.text: In a large bowl, toss {{ingredients}} until the chocolate pieces are distributed through the brioche. The remaining third of the dark chocolate belongs to the chocolate custard.

steps.title: Make the chocolate cream
steps.text: In a saucepan over low heat, whisk {{ingredients}} until the chocolate has melted and the mixture is smooth. Stir frequently, scraping the bottom; do not scorch or boil the cream.

steps.title: Cool the chocolate mixture
steps.text: Transfer the chocolate cream to a large bowl. Whisk in {{ingredients}} until smooth; let it cool to lukewarm before adding the eggs.

steps.title: Add eggs and vanilla
steps.text: In a second bowl, whisk {{ingredients}} just until blended, then whisk in the lukewarm chocolate dairy mixture until uniform. Use the full listed cream and milk in this custard.

steps.title: Soak the brioche fully
steps.text: Pour the complete chocolate custard over the bread mixture and fold gently to wet every cube. Let stand for about 30 minutes, folding once or twice, until the bread has absorbed custard and no dry centers remain. Keep total room-temperature handling of the raw egg mixture within 2 hours, or 1 hour above 90°F; cover and refrigerate if the wait will extend. Heat the oven to 325°F during the soak.

steps.title: Divide the full mixture
steps.text: Stir gently before each scoop so every dish gets bread, chocolate and custard. Divide the entire mixture among the prepared cups, keeping the stated headroom. If it will not fit the cups, use the prepared extra dish. A larger-dish batch follows the same complete ingredient allocation; do not discard custard or chocolate to make a vessel fit.

steps.title: Bake by each center
steps.text: Bake cups at 325°F, starting the first center checks around 30 minutes; roughly 35–60 minutes is a planning range for these roomy cups. For the 2-quart dish, start checking around 45 minutes and plan roughly 45–60 minutes, continuing as needed. The middle must be set with no liquid custard wave and reach at least 160°F in the egg custard, away from a melted chocolate pocket and the dish. A moist bread crumb and melted chocolate can look wet, so use both the texture and the temperature. Check each dish independently and shield a darkening top loosely with foil.

steps.title: Rest and serve warm
steps.text: Rest on a rack for 10 minutes so the custard settles, then serve warm with {{ingredients}}, shared across the batch. Refrigerate leftover pudding within 2 hours of cooking, or 1 hour above 90°F; keep the ice cream in the freezer.

learning.focus: Hydrate weighed brioche with chocolate custard and bake each center gently.
learning.outcome: Soft custard-soaked brioche with dark chocolate depth, sweet white-chocolate pockets and cold vanilla ice cream.
before: Weigh the brioche and keep the complete measured formula together when changing the batch.
Measure cup capacity with water before choosing the dishes. Use cups of at least 12 fluid ounces, leave the stated headroom and use enough dishes for the full batch.
Warm the chocolate dairy gently, then cool it to lukewarm before adding eggs. All cream goes into the custard.

checkpoints.cue: The chocolate dairy is smooth and lukewarm.
checkpoints.why: Hot cream can curdle eggs as they are mixed.

checkpoints.cue: Every bread cube is moistened and its center is no longer dry.
checkpoints.why: The soak distributes custard instead of leaving dry brioche within a cooked outer layer.

checkpoints.cue: The egg custard is set without a liquid wave and reaches at least 160°F in each dish.
checkpoints.why: Cup depth, melted chocolate and a browned surface can conceal a cooler center.

troubleshooting.problem: The middle is liquid while the top darkens.
troubleshooting.cause: The cup is deep or the oven browns the surface quickly.
troubleshooting.fix: Shield the top loosely with foil and continue at 325°F until the center checks agree. Check dishes separately.

troubleshooting.problem: Dry bread remains after the soak.
troubleshooting.cause: The custard did not reach all the cubes or the bread was overpacked.
troubleshooting.fix: Fold gently and press dry cubes into the existing custard; extend the soak under refrigeration if needed. Keep the weighed formula rather than guessing an extra dairy dose.

learning.storage: Refrigerate pudding in shallow portions at 40°F or below within 2 hours of cooking, or 1 hour above 90°F; do not leave the full bake on the counter until completely cold. Cover once cool and use within 3–4 days. Reheat the pudding to 165°F in the center, keeping ice cream separate and frozen. Freeze cooled portions promptly for longer storage and thaw in the refrigerator. If preparing the raw soaked mixture ahead, cover and refrigerate promptly and bake within 12 hours; choose oven-safe dishes suitable for a chilled start and continue until the same center endpoints are reached.
learning.timing: Allow about 25–35 minutes for weighing, chopping and making the chocolate custard, then about 30 minutes soaking and 10 minutes post-bake rest. Cup baking starts from roughly 35–60 minutes at 325°F; a larger 2-quart dish starts from 45–60 minutes. Cold starts or deeper vessels can extend both plans. When scaling, keep every ingredient ratio and chocolate share together and add appropriate vessels or oven loads; do not multiply dimensions, heat or time. For a fractional egg quantity, beat an egg and weigh out the required fraction rather than rounding the egg count.

exactAfter.body:
## Chef's Note

Brioche absorbs a chocolate custard while bittersweet and white chocolate leave contrasting pockets in the crumb. Weigh the bread, let every cube soak through, and bake each center gently. Serve the warm pudding with cold vanilla ice cream.

## Directions

1. **Choose dishes with room for the full batch:** Use oven-safe individual soufflé cups with at least 12 fluid ounces (1½ cups) capacity each. Coat them with nonstick cooking spray and set them on a rimmed baking sheet. Use enough cups for the whole batch. Fill no cup above three-quarters of its capacity after soaking, and have an extra cup or small dish ready if needed. For a larger pudding, use a coated 2-quart baking dish only if the complete soaked mixture fits with space below its rim; use an extra dish for any excess.
2. **Combine the bread and chocolate pieces:** In a large bowl, toss brioche, 2/3 of the bittersweet chocolate (70% cacao), and white chocolate chips until the chocolate pieces are distributed through the brioche. The remaining third of the dark chocolate belongs to the chocolate custard.
3. **Make the chocolate cream:** In a saucepan over low heat, whisk 1/3 of the bittersweet chocolate (70% cacao), heavy cream, unsweetened cocoa powder, and granulated sugar until the chocolate has melted and the mixture is smooth. Stir frequently, scraping the bottom; do not scorch or boil the cream.
4. **Cool the chocolate mixture:** Transfer the chocolate cream to a large bowl. Whisk in whole milk until smooth; let it cool to lukewarm before adding the eggs.
5. **Add eggs and vanilla:** In a second bowl, whisk large eggs, fine salt, and vanilla extract just until blended, then whisk in the lukewarm chocolate dairy mixture until uniform. Use the full listed cream and milk in this custard.
6. **Soak the brioche fully:** Pour the complete chocolate custard over the bread mixture and fold gently to wet every cube. Let stand for about 30 minutes, folding once or twice, until the bread has absorbed custard and no dry centers remain. Keep total room-temperature handling of the raw egg mixture within 2 hours, or 1 hour above 90°F; cover and refrigerate if the wait will extend. Heat the oven to 325°F during the soak.
7. **Divide the full mixture:** Stir gently before each scoop so every dish gets bread, chocolate and custard. Divide the entire mixture among the prepared cups, keeping the stated headroom. If it will not fit the cups, use the prepared extra dish. A larger-dish batch follows the same complete ingredient allocation; do not discard custard or chocolate to make a vessel fit.
8. **Bake by each center:** Bake cups at 325°F, starting the first center checks around 30 minutes; roughly 35–60 minutes is a planning range for these roomy cups. For the 2-quart dish, start checking around 45 minutes and plan roughly 45–60 minutes, continuing as needed. The middle must be set with no liquid custard wave and reach at least 160°F in the egg custard, away from a melted chocolate pocket and the dish. A moist bread crumb and melted chocolate can look wet, so use both the texture and the temperature. Check each dish independently and shield a darkening top loosely with foil.
9. **Rest and serve warm:** Rest on a rack for 10 minutes so the custard settles, then serve warm with vanilla bean ice cream, shared across the batch. Refrigerate leftover pudding within 2 hours of cooking, or 1 hour above 90°F; keep the ice cream in the freezer.

findings.scope: Whole recipe with disclosed source-versus-adaptation choices
findings.exactBeforeAfter: See exactBefore and exactAfter for complete cooking text and all changed fields
rationale: This is an explicitly new measured adaptation, not a recovered or certified Ritz-Carlton formula. The saved 13-cup bread/cream-reservation/eight-6-ounce-cup conflict remains in the exact private original; it is not rewritten or used as the new ratio authority.
King Arthur’s complete primary formula supplies 453 g/1 lb brioche, three cups total dairy, six eggs, cocoa, salt, a 30-minute soak, 325°F baking and a 2-quart larger-dish route.

The selected dairy is 1½ cups cream plus 1½ cups whole milk, a richer contemporary choice within the same total liquid quantity; the cream is fully allocated to custard. No original reservation is inferred.

All six ounces each of bittersweet and white chocolate and two cups vanilla ice cream are retained as a deliberate rich double-chocolate adaptation. One third of the dark chocolate melts into cream; the remainder and all white chips remain in the bread. This changes the primary’s chocolate amount and types, rather than falsely claiming its exact formula.

The current ¾-cup total sugar is retained entirely in the custard; its old topping allocation is removed. Cocoa and fine salt come from the new complete primary basis. The source’s one-cup sugar is not used because white chocolate adds sweetness; this flavor-balancing decision is editorial, not a historical or tested measurement.

Bon Appétit supplies a complete individual chocolate-pudding precedent at 325°F with six 8–10-ounce ramekins and 40-minute baking for its own different formula. The proposed roomier ≥12-ounce cups, three-quarter fill ceiling and 35–60-minute plan are conservative modern operating choices for this larger/richer batch, not its original vessel/yield certification.

The larger 2-quart route is supported by King Arthur’s actual complete method, but the added chocolate means actual fit and center checks still govern. Its timing is separate from the individual route.
FDA/USDA safety guidance supersedes the source’s five-day fridge guidance. The original 12-hour make-ahead note is retained under prompt refrigeration; no fermentation/preservation claim.
